newsitem.title: RUSSIA: UK's Cook, in Moscow, unrepentant on Bosnia swoop.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook, in Moscow, unrepentant on Bosnia swoop.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook arrived in Moscow early on Monday, unrepentant in the face of fierce Russian criticism of a swoop by NATO peacekeepers on suspected Bosnian war criminals.

Cook was due to hold talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, who made no secret of his unhappiness with the NATO raid when he met U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in St Petersburg at the weekend.

In last Thursday's carefully planned operation, British special forces shot dead Simo Drljaca, a prominent police chief, after he resisted arrest and opened fire on them. They also seized a hospital director and extradited him to The Hague.

Both had been the subject of sealed war crimes indictments by a U.N. Tribunal, but Primakov said Russia was worried that the action could undermine Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic. The West is backing Plavsic in a power struggle with former Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, himself indicted of war crimes.
Cook told reporters who flew him to Moscow that he would explore Russia's anxieties in his talks with Primakov but would express no regrets.
"On Bosnia, he will find me diplomatic but unrepentant," Cook said.

He said British forces had acted squarely in accordance with the mandate given to the United Nations peacekeeping force in Bosnia, SFOR, which has instructions to apprehend any suspected war criminals it comes across.
Cook said SFOR's mandate had not changed but acknowledged there was a greater readiness on the part of Britain and the United States, in particular, to act on it.

"There is a new resoluteness in international circles," said the foreign secretary, the first British cabinet minister to visit Moscow since Labour won the May 1 election, ending 18 years of Conservative rule in Britain.
NATO and bilateral cooperation are the other main topics on the agenda for Cook, who will also meet First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.

Britain is keen to allay Russian fears about NATO's enlargement to include former communist nations of Eastern Europe. It wants to breathe life into a fledgling partnership council established in May as part of a landmark treaty between Moscow and the western defence alliance.

Cook said he would propose to Primakov that the council, designed to give Moscow a say but not a veto in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's affairs, concentrate on just a few areas on a long list of potential spheres of cooperation.
These might include steps to curb weapons proliferation in the Middle East, notably Iran and Iraq, Cook said.
On the bilateral front, Cook hopes to finalise the details of an agreement on closer cooperation between Britain and Russia in the fight against crime, drugs and terrorism.
The pact, involving closer liaison between the two countries' police and intelligence services, is due to be signed by Prime Minister Tony Blair in Moscow this autumn.
